title: #21 Don't give exam papers or homework back before whole class feedback
author: Barton, Craig
summary: Craig Barton opens with a familiar classroom scenario: handing back marked assessments before whole-class feedback triggers a scramble over grades, and students who already know they got a question right or wrong mentally check out before the teacher even begins explaining it. His fix is to withhold the papers until after the problematic questions have been addressed as a class, which preserves both focus and students' incentive to engage since no one yet knows their own results. He layers on a second move, tied to his earlier "Myth of Copying Things Down" argument: rather than letting students passively watch and copy a worked solution, he has them attempt a similar follow-up question on mini-whiteboards immediately after the explanation, which gives him real evidence of whether the explanation landed. The piece is a two-part practical fix to a common feedback routine, aimed at preserving attention and generating actual evidence of understanding rather than assuming it from passive copying.
points: Handing assessments back before whole-class feedback predictably triggers a scramble over marks and causes students to mentally check out of questions they already know they got right or wrong.
Withholding papers until after addressing the problematic questions preserves attention because no student yet knows their own result, creating a shared incentive to engage.

Passively copying a modeled solution doesn't demonstrate understanding; following an explanation immediately with a similar question (ideally on mini-whiteboards) generates real evidence of whether it landed.
The approach is framed as a workload-effective replacement for writing individual feedback comments on every student's paper, which Barton says used to take hours and be routinely ignored.
quotes: All of a sudden students begin obsessing about their marks and the marks of their mates.
Josh has a look through his paper and sees he has got Question 3 correct, and so promptly switches off and starts flicking bits of rubber at Ben.

It is far superior in terms of effectiveness and workload to what I used to do for most of my career: write individual feedback on each student’s work that would take hours and subsequently be ignored.
As soon as you give students their assessments back before diving into whole-class feedback, you lose a lot of time and attention in the ways described above.
Just because students watch you go through how to do a tricky question and then copy it into their books does not mean they understand it.
This follow-up question provides an extra incentive for students to listen hard to your explanation and provides you with some evidence that the explanation you have given makes sense.
